nodes.label: Somali alphabet: a b c d dh e f g h i j k kh l m n o q r s sh t u w x y '
b: pronounced as in English; at end of words may sound like p without aspiration
d: tongue further forward than English, touching the teeth
dh: curling tongue back; between vowels softened to r-type sound; in Mogadishu pronounced as r
q: voiced uvular plosive, made at back of mouth where uvular drops down
t: same as English but never found at end of syllables
k: same as English but never found at end of syllables
j: may be pronounced like ch in church or j in jingle
kh: like Scottish loch; only in Arabic loanwords
x: voiceless pharyngeal fricative, made in pharynx with contraction
c: made in same part as x but with vocal cord vibration (Arabic 'ayn)
m: does not occur at end of syllables except before b or m
r: rolled r, often breathy; similar to Italian
Geminate consonants in Somali: b, d, dh, g, l, m, n, r
Geminate consonants held longer and are stronger; written by doubling the letter
a: pronounced as in English bat, more open than southern England
e: pronounced as in English red
i: pronounced as in English bit
o: pronounced as in English top, sometimes slightly fronted
u: pronounced as in English put
Long vowels written with double letters, pronounced about twice as long
Diphthongs in Somali: ay, aw, ey, oy, ow; ay and ey generally interchangeable
Stress-tone: vowel pronounced at slightly higher pitch and stressed more; marked by acute accent
Stress-tone placed on vowel units: short vowel = 1 unit; long vowels and diphthongs = 2 units
Long vowel with stress on first part = falling pitch; stress on second part = rising/same pitch
See-saw stress-tone: if following word has stress-tone, no stress on waa/mi; if no following stress-tone, stress on circumflex vowel
t and k never occur at end of syllables; change to d and g respectively at syllable boundary
m cannot occur at end of word; changes to n
t changes to d after gutturals (q, kh, c, x, h, ')
t changes to d after w, y, or any vowel
t changes to dh after dh (geminate)
m changes to l after l
m changes to r after r
y inserted between verb ending in -i and vowel-initial ending
Short vowel a plus guttural changes to e before -een ending (assimilation)
Some verb final consonants alternate: e.g., bug 'be ill' → g becomes k before vowel endings
dh when geminate always written dh (never dhdh)
Past tense ending -ay may be written -ey; spelling not standardized
Singular imperative = basic form of verb = dictionary form; stress-tone on penultimate/only vowel
Plural imperative: add -a to singular; if verb ends in -i, insert y (-ya)
Third person object pronouns (it/him/her/them) have no overt translation in Somali
Ma...baa? asks 'Is it...?' questions; answered with waa
General past tense: imperative form + past endings (-ay, -tay, -nay, -teen, -een)
General past tense has no stress-tone on any vowels in main clauses
Imperative stress-tone deleted when used as base for other forms
waa is positive declarative mood classifier; use is obligatory in positive declarative sentences; see-saw stress-tone
Verbal subject pronouns cannot stand alone; must be used with mood classifier or focus marker
waa combines with subject pronouns: w- added to beginning, long vowel -aa deleted
Two 'we' forms: inclusive (including hearer) -aynu; exclusive (excluding hearer) -aannu
waa may stand alone; implies third person subject pronoun according to verb ending
Vocative feminine: add -ay to name/noun; final vowel deleted
Vocative masculine: add -ow to name/noun; final vowel deleted
No informal/formal address distinction in Somali; imperative used for all
No word for 'please' in Somali; imperative use is not rude
miyaa equivalent to ma...baa for questions
Present progressive: verb stem + progressive marker -ay- + present tense endings
Present progressive stress-tone on vowel immediately before progressive marker -ay-
t changes to s when present ending beginning with -t- follows progressive marker -ay-
y inserted between verb ending in -i and progressive marker -ay-
Present progressive may also express near future: 'I am going to'
Nouns have two genders: masculine and feminine; gender must be learnt with noun
Plural gender often different from singular: e.g., naag (f.sg) → naago (m.pl); inan (m.sg) → inammo (f.pl)
Declension members share: plural formation, plural gender, stress-tone pattern, singular gender tendency
Declension 1: singular mostly feminine, plural always masculine; word shape: does not end in -o; plural: add -o
Declension 1: singular ends in -i → plural add -yo
Declension 2: singular mostly masculine, plural always feminine; mostly more than one syllable, not ending in -e
Declension 2: singular ends in guttural, j, or s → add -yo
Declension 2: singular ends in b, d, dh, r, l, or n → consonant doubled in plural
Declension 2: singular ends in n → may change to m (geminated)
Declension 3: singular masc. or fem., plural always masc.; word shape: (C)hV(V)CVC; add -o and delete final vowel
Declension 3: final consonant may change because basic form sound cannot occur at end of syllable
-na: attached to first grammatical unit of second sentence; joins positive declarative/imperative sentences
iyo: joins nouns or noun phrases; with lists of >2 nouns, iyo between last two only
Definite article: suffix beginning with k- for masculine, t- for feminine; vowel depends on context and case
Definite article forms: absolutive -ka/-ta; subject -ku/-tu; anaphoric/known -kii/-tii
-kii/-tii: used when noun previously referred to, in past, or known to speaker/hearer
-ka/-ta: used when noun first mentioned, unknown, or in future/present
Feminine article sound changes: same as verb -t- endings (pp.18-19); noun ending in o: t→d and o→a
Masculine article: k disappears after gutturals (q, kh, c, x, h, '); short a changes to article vowel
Masculine article: k changes to h after any vowel except i; final vowel changes to article vowel (short)
Masculine article: k changes to g after g, i, w, or y
Somali word order: Subject-Object-Verb (SOV); mood classifier comes as close to verb as possible
Adverbial words generally at beginning of sentence (may also come at end)
Premodifier form: plural of declensions 1, 2, 3 takes stress-tone on final vowel
Declension 4: singular always masc., plural always masc.; one syllable ending in consonant; plural: add -a and copy consonant
Declension 4 exception: wiil 'boy, son' → wiilal (pl.) but feminine, thus wiilasha
Declension 5: singular always masc., plural always fem.; 1-3 syllables, never 1 syllable with 1 short vowel; plural: gender and stress-tone change only
Focus markers: baa and ayaa; replace waa in focused sentences; noun before focus marker is focused
Focus markers combine with subject pronouns: baa → buu/bay/etc.; ayaa → ayuu/ayay/etc.
Causative suffix: -i added to basic form changes intransitive to transitive verb meaning 'cause to'
Causative: if suffix added to verb ending in g or q, consonant changes to j
Causative: if -i added to verb ending in vowel a plus guttural, a changes to i (vowel assimilation)
Conjugation 2A plural imperative: add -ya to base form (verbs ending in -i)
Conjugation 2A general past: base form + endings; t→s, y inserted between i and a, n geminated in 1pl
Conjugation 2A infinitive: base form + -in (with stress-tone on i)
Conjugation 2A present progressive: infinitive form + progressive -ay- + present endings
Possessive suffixes have subject case forms: e.g., -ay (abs.) → -ay (subj. fem. noun); -kiis (abs.) → -iis (subj.)

Lesson 3: Bill iyo Zaynab (Bill and Zaynab)
Lesson 4: Bill waa tegayaa geeska Afrika (Bill is going to the Horn of Africa)

nodes.label: Plural adjectives are formed by taking the largest possible syllable from the beginning of the adjective and adding it to the beginning of the singular form; single-syllable adjectives are repeated.
Feminine singular nouns not ending in -o often add -eéd in the genitive; this implies less specific reference.
Feminine singular nouns forming plural in -o add -od when the plural is in the genitive case.
Nouns for domestic animals use -aad instead of -eéd or -od in the genitive.
Nouns occurring with numbers are in genitive singular unless from declension 1, 2, or 3 (then genitive plural), except with the number one.
When the definite article is used with a noun-number combination, the definite article is added to the number.
kow = counting; hal = counting nouns; mid = referring to one on its own.
Conjugation 1 verbs whose stem ends in a vowel delete that vowel when an ending beginning with a vowel is added.
The vowel is also deleted when the vowel of the progressive marker follows the stem.
Most irregular plurals are Arabic loanwords; they may also take Somali plurals alongside Arabic ones.
Most irregular nouns reverse their gender in the plural.
Conjugation 1 general present: verb stem + endings (aa, taa, aa, taa, naa, taan, aan); stress-tone on penultimate vowel.
Conjugation 2A general present: verb stem + aa/ endings with y inserted before a vowel endings; n geminated in 1pl.
Conjugation 2B general present: verb stem + aa/ endings; y inserted between double vowel and a vowel ending.
Object pronoun comes before preverbal prepositions: OBJECT PRONOUN + PREVERBAL PREPOSITION + VERB.
Ordinal numbers are formed by adding -aad to the cardinal number; some numbers lose a vowel.
Question word max- combines with subject pronouns: max+aan, max+aad, max+uu, max+ay, etc.
baa and ayaa are interchangeable focus markers with no difference in meaning; they emphasize a particular noun phrase.
The focus marker follows the focused noun phrase; subject clitics may follow the focus marker.
When subject is focused: the subject is in absolutive case; subject verbal pronoun is not used; reduced verb paradigm is used.
Reduced paradigm = same as full forms except: long final aa → short a; stress-tone on final vowel; reduced person/number distinctions.
baa contracts with preceding noun ending in short vowel: ninka + baa → ninkaa.
Conjugation 3B differs from 3A: if verb ends in -do, d deleted before vowel endings; present progressive uses infinitive form.
Conjugation 3B plural imperative: -ta replaces -o of the stem.
Number combinations: first number in premodifier form + iyo + second number.
Tell time: use number with definite article; -ka/-ta for future reference, -kii/-tii for past reference.
Conjugation 1 infinitive: add -i to base form; stress-tone on penultimate vowel.
Single-syllable verb with vowel a changes to e in infinitive (except with guttural consonant → i).
Single-syllable verb with vowel a and final guttural: a changes to i.
Future tense: infinitive of main verb + doon in general present tense.
Habitual past ('used to'): infinitive of main verb + jir in general past tense.
Negative imperative conj 2/3: ha + infinitive; optional -nin in singular, required in plural.
Negative imperative conj 1: ha + infinitive + -n; stress-tone on penultimate vowel.
Negative general past: ma + negative verb form (same as negative imperative for conj 2/3); stress-tone on final vowel for conj 1.
ma combines with subject pronouns: ma+aan → maan, ma+aad → ma'ad, ma+uu → mu'uu, ma+ay → may, etc.
Negative future: auxiliary doon in negative general present (same as negating general present).
Negative general present: ma + negative verb form.
Subject forms: -kani/-tani or -kanu/-tanu; no difference in meaning between -i and -u.
Past progressive: same formation as present progressive but with past tense endings instead of present.
rab as auxiliary with infinitive expresses 'want to do'; in general present tense.
kar as auxiliary with infinitive expresses 'be able to do'.
waa as auxiliary with infinitive expresses 'fail to do' or simple negation; way- before consonant endings.
When ending beginning with vowel is added to waa, y is inserted: waa+ay → waayay.
When ending beginning with consonant is added, waa- changes to way-: waa+tay → wayday.
Impersonal pronoun la is placed immediately before object verbal pronouns.
Impersonal la is used to translate English passive constructions.
Positive declarative sentence must have a mood classifier (waa) or focus marker (baa/ayaa) to be correct.
When an adjective describes the possessed noun (not the possessor), use ee after the adjective.

nodes.statement: Possessive suffixes consist of possessive suffix proper + definite article suffix. The definite article shows case difference.
When possessive suffix is added to a noun denoting a relative or body part, the possessive suffix on its own is used without the definite article part.
The -ii type definite article endings may be used in possessive suffixes where appropriate for referential definiteness.
Possessive suffixes are used with nouns of position and time to form phrases translating as prepositions (e.g., gudahayda 'inside me/it').
Each prepositional phrase has masculine and feminine forms according to the noun going with the phrase.
Both types of genitive constructions are equally used in Somali: noun+possessive suffix and noun+noun.
Negative present progressive: change positive present tense endings to negative present tense endings (familiar from general present) and use with ma.
Alternative negative present progressive: auxiliary form (maayo/maysid/mayso etc.) immediately follows the infinitive.
Negative past progressive: use ma with unchanging form verb+ayn or verb+aynin (conjugation 1: stem+ayn/in; conjugations 2-3: infinitive+ayn/in).
There are five prefixing verbs where person marker is added as a prefix: yiil, yimi, yidhi, yiqiin, yahay.
jir stresses that a thing exists; yiil stresses that an object is in a particular place; joog is used for animate subjects in a place.
When plural endings are added to yimi, the final -i of the stem is deleted (yimaaddeen/timaaddeen).
The infinitive of yimi is iman, used with auxiliary verbs and as base for progressive aspect.
yidhi is used only with direct speech. Indirect speech uses sheeg with an in-clause.
To translate 'to' as in 'I said to him', the preverbal preposition ku is used.
Basic word order of waxa-focus construction: WAXA (+verbal pronoun) VERB FOCUSED NOUN PHRASE.
When subject is focused with waxa: subject is in absolutive form, verb uses reduced paradigm, waxa lacks subject verbal pronoun.
Subordinate clauses are all essentially noun phrases and can play the same roles as noun phrases in a sentence.
Mood classifiers and focus markers are not used in subordinate clauses; negative word is aan instead of ma.
All subordinate clauses are essentially relative clauses.
In in-clauses, case marking goes on the final verb since it is the last part of the subordinate clause noun phrase.
Word order in in-clauses: SUBJECT OBJECT VERB (object may also come after verb).
General present and present progressive subordinate forms are the same as main clause negative forms: -aa changes to -o, -aan to -aan.
General past and past progressive subordinate forms differ from main clause only in stress-tone pattern.
'In order to' is rendered by an in-clause with preverbal preposition u.
'Have to, must' is rendered by in-clause with classifier waa (waa in...).
Fixed order in preposition/pronoun clusters: PRONOUN + PREPOSITIONS (in order: u, ku, ka, la).
Whenever a preverbal preposition is in a cluster with pronouns or other preverbal prepositions, there is only one stress-tone on the final vowel.
Restrictive relative clauses use oo; appositive (non-restrictive) relative clauses use ee.
oo is not a relative pronoun; there is no relative pronoun in Somali. oo only distinguishes clause types.
Appositive relative clauses cannot be used with undefined head nouns.
Restrictive relative clauses may not be used with names.
In relative clauses when subject is a pronoun, subject verbal pronouns are used on their own (no classifier or focus marker).
When head noun is not subject of RC and RC is not subject of sentence: present = main clause negative forms; past = stress-tone on final vowel, reduced paradigm absolutive.
When head noun is not subject of RC but RC is subject of sentence: verb form same as main clause in all respects (subject marking on verb).
When head noun is subject of RC and RC is not subject of main sentence: reduced paradigm (absolutive) is used.
When head noun is subject of RC and RC is subject of main sentence: reduced paradigm (subject) with main clause endings.
When a subject relative clause is focused, the verb is not marked as subject because the RC is focused.
When yaa is subject of sentence, reduced paradigm is used (incorporates focus marker baa).
When answering questions, the information asked for must be focused.
Independent pronouns may be used for emphasis and for focusing a pronoun.
Independent pronouns are basically nouns with the definite article suffix attached (all masculine except iyada).
'While' construction: independent pronoun + appositive relative clause with oo joined to pronoun.
General past of yahay has no person marker prefix; person marker appears as suffix (aha, ahayd, ahayn, etc.).
General present of yahay uses person marker prefixes; stem changes from ah to i in 2nd/3rd plural.
Reduced paradigm of yahay present: invariable ah (absolutive) and ihi (subject).
There is no progressive form of yahay because it is a stative verb.
Subordinate clause forms of yahay are the same as main clause forms except reduced paradigm past tense (subject form without stress-tone).
Predicative adjectives use yahay as a copula; predicative adjectives can be written separately from or joined to yahay.
Short forms of yahay with adjectives: delete ah from the full form (e.g., dheer yahay -> dheeryay).
Attributive adjectives with yahay in relative clauses: zero/nothing is the absolutive form (adjective alone), -i is the subject form.
Comparative is formed with preverbal preposition ka + adjective.
Superlative is formed with preverbal preposition cluster ugu + adjective.
'Very' is expressed with aad + ii + adjective; aad is focused with baa or ayaa.
For further emphasis, use aad iyo aad ('very very').
Stress-tone pattern of adjectives is almost always stress-tone on the final vowel.
'Which' is expressed with suffix -kee (m.) / -tee (f.). When used on its own means 'which one(s)?'.
'Where' uses xaggee or halkee with -kee suffix, or mee on its own.

nodes.statement: Shortened forms of yahay in general present are formed by deleting the ah part in the middle. Pattern: person marker + ay = ending (e.g., -tay, -yay, -nay, -tiin, -yiin).
In the negative, shortened versions are optional and formed by deleting ah from the full negative general present form.
When yahay is used with adjectives in subordinate clauses, the contracted form of the verb is ALWAYS used, in both present and past tense.
The comparative is formed using the preverbal preposition ka with the adjective. The adjective retains its yahay agreement.
The superlative is expressed using the preverbal preposition cluster ugu with the adjective. Ugu may be used on its own with adjectives.
To express 'very', use aad with preverbal preposition i. The word aad must always be focused using baa or ayaa.
The suffix -kee/-tee is used for 'which'. -kee is added to masculine nouns and -tee to feminine nouns. Usually focused.
'Where' is expressed with xaggee (from xag 'place') or halkee (from hal 'place'). Answer must focus the location.
Mass nouns are used with a form of yahay (typically ah) in a relative clause construction. When a number precedes the unit of measure, oo is used.
Collective nouns behave the same way as mass nouns and take the same yahay relative clause construction.
Adverbial conjunctions (when, if, after, etc.) are translated by relative clauses with specific head nouns functioning like conjunctions. Subject verbal pronoun added to the head noun.
When is rendered by marka with relative clause; subject verbal pronoun added to marka. Markii (with -kii definite) may also be used, with pronoun written separately.
The negative word in subordinate clauses is aan (not ma). Aan immediately follows the head noun and is attached if the noun ends in a short vowel. In appositive relative clauses, aan follows oo.
Shortened subject verbal pronouns used with aan: -aynu (I/we incl.), -aad (you sg.), -aannu (we excl.), -aydin (you pl.), -ay (he/she/they). First three differ from main clause forms.
The negative form using maayoo cannot be used in relative clauses for present progressive. Use keenayo, keenayse, etc., or the invariable past progressive form keenayn/keenaynin.
For focusing in yes-no questions with baa: Ma NP baa ...? When subject is focused, all characteristics from statements also apply in questions.
For focusing in yes-no questions with miyaa: NP miyaa/d + subject verbal pronoun ...? If subject is focused, familiar characteristics (reduced paradigm) are present.
Negative questions without noun phrase focus use sew...ma: Sew maad tegin? (Didn't you go?) Sew may be separated from ma by intervening noun phrases.
If a noun phrase is focused in a negative question, aan is added to the focus marker. Shortened subject verbal pronouns are used with negative + focus combinations.
Optative: pronoun (inherent part except 3rd person) + verb stem + ending. Endings: -o (1SG/3SG.M), -to (2SG/3SG.F), -no (1PL), -teen (2PL), -een (3PL). 3rd person uses ha + verb.
Optative stress-tone is on the vowel immediately before the ending, except 3rd person where stress-tone is on ha instead.
Negative optative uses invariable verb form (same as negative general past, stress-tone on final vowel of stem for conjugation 1). Preceded by negative words incorporating subject pronouns.
Potential: verb stem + ee/ee endings with vowel harmony. Endings: -ee (1SG/3SG.M), -tee (2SG/3SG.F), -nee (1PL), -teen (2PL), -een (3PL). Classifier shuw always present.

Conditional 'would have': infinitive + leh with contracted yahay forms. No tense distinction. Forms: lahaa (1SG/3SG.M), lahayd (2SG/3SG.F), lahayn (1PL.INCL), lahaydeen (2PL), lahaayeen (3PL/1PL.EXCL).
Negative conditional uses ma + infinitive + -een/teén endings. Pattern parallels conditional affirmative but with negative marker ma.
Reduced paradigm is used when the head noun is the subject of the relative clause. All verbs follow the same reduced pattern regardless of conjugation.
Full paradigm (absolutive) used when head noun is NOT the subject of the relative clause and head noun + clause is NOT the subject of the main clause.
Full paradigm (subject) used when head noun is NOT the subject of the relative clause but head noun + clause IS the subject of the main clause. Same as main clause full paradigm.
The pronoun la ('one') behaves like na in clusters but must come before any object pronoun.
Possessive suffixes have short versions without the definite article. Masculine: kay/kaa/kiis/keed/keen/kayo/kin/kood. Feminine: tay/taa/tiis/teed/teen/tayo/tiin/tiod.
Note the geminate bb in the verb cab: the b is geminated when an ending beginning with a vowel follows.

nodes.name: Somali Alphabet Size
nodes.description: The Somali alphabet contains 26 letters plus the glottal stop (hamza). Native Somali words never use p, v, z.

nodes.name: Vowel Length Contrast
nodes.description: Somali has five short vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and five long vowels (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu). Vowel length is phonemically significant.

nodes.name: Consonant Doubling Contrast
nodes.description: Somali distinguishes short and long (doubled) consonants: e.g., abaar (drought) vs abbaar (aim at).

nodes.name: Glottal Stop Position
nodes.description: The glottal stop (hamza) can never be word-initial in Somali.

nodes.name: Tone and Grammatical Gender
nodes.description: In Somali, tone is used to distinguish grammatical gender. Words spelled the same in root form are distinguished by different gender endings and/or tone.

nodes.name: Focus Marker Position
nodes.description: baa marks FOCUS (new or emphasized information) and comes AFTER the head noun.

nodes.name: Declarative Marker Position
nodes.description: waa marks positive declarative statements and comes BEFORE the head noun/predicate.

nodes.name: Question Marker Function
nodes.description: ma marks positive (non-negative) yes/no questions.

nodes.name: Grammatical Gender is Arbitrary
nodes.description: Somali is a language based on grammatical gender. The way a noun is handled does not always make semantic sense. Gender has far-reaching grammatical impact on plural forms and verb agreement.

nodes.name: Masculine Article -ka
nodes.description: Masculine nouns take article suffixes beginning with -k. The standard form -ka marks NEW INFORMATION. The form -kii marks GIVEN/PREVIOUSLY KNOWN information.

nodes.name: Feminine Article -ta
nodes.description: Feminine nouns take article suffixes beginning with -t. The standard form -ta marks NEW INFORMATION. The form -tii marks GIVEN/PREVIOUSLY KNOWN information.

nodes.name: Four Forms per Noun
nodes.description: Each Somali noun ultimately requires learning four forms: (1) singular root, (2) with article, (3) plural form, (4) plural with article.

nodes.name: Masculine Noun: -e to -a
nodes.description: With masculine nouns ending in -e, the final vowel changes to -a and the article changes to -ha: fure → furaha.

nodes.name: Masculine Noun: -e to -i (known)
nodes.description: With masculine nouns ending in -e, for known information, the final vowel changes to -i and the article changes to -hii: fure → furihii.

nodes.name: Masculine Noun: -o to -a
nodes.description: With masculine nouns ending in -o, the final vowel changes to -a and the article changes to -ha: biyo → biyaha.

nodes.name: Masculine Noun: -o to -i (known)
nodes.description: With masculine nouns ending in -o, for known information, the final vowel changes to -i and the article changes to -hii: biyo → biyihii.

nodes.name: k→g Assimilation
nodes.description: If a masculine noun ends in -g, -w, -y, or -i, the k of the article changes to g: buug → buugga, guri → guriga.

nodes.name: k Drops After Certain Consonants
nodes.description: If a masculine noun ends in -c, -h, -q, -kh, or -x, the k of the article is lost, leaving only the vowel: magac → magaca, shaah → shaaha, suuq → suuqa, madax → madaxa.

nodes.name: Vowel Harmony in Masculine Nouns
nodes.description: The final vowel of the root changes to match the vowel of the suffix (e→a with -ha, e→i with -hii, o→a with -ha, o→i with -hii).

nodes.name: Feminine Noun: -o to -a
nodes.description: With feminine nouns ending in -o, the final vowel changes to -a and the article changes to -da: cunto → cuntada.

nodes.name: Feminine t→d Change
nodes.description: If a feminine noun ends in a vowel (other than -o) or with -d, -h, -kh, -x, -w, -y, or glottal stop, the t changes to d: mindi → mindida, subax → subaxda.

nodes.name: Feminine t→dha Change
nodes.description: In dialects with feminine nouns ending in -dh, the -ta suffix changes to -dha: gabadh → gabadhdha. In other dialects these words end in -r.

nodes.name: l + t → sh Assimilation
nodes.description: When a feminine noun ends in -l, the combination of final -l plus suffix -t changes both sounds to -sh-: basal + ta → basasha, il + ta → isha, meel + ta → meesha.

nodes.name: Vowel Harmony in Feminine Nouns
nodes.description: The final vowel -o of the root changes to -a to match the suffix vowel -a: cunto → cuntada, daawo → daawada.

nodes.name: Singular Imperative as Citation Form
nodes.description: The singular imperative is the main citation form for each verb; needed to find a verb in a Somali dictionary and upon which most other tenses are built.

nodes.name: Plural Imperative with -a
nodes.description: The plural imperative is generally formed by adding -a to the singular imperative (for consonant-final verbs): gal → gala, bax → baxa.

nodes.name: Plural Imperative with -ya
nodes.description: If a verb ends in -i or -e, add -ya to form the plural imperative: akhri → akhriya, sii → siiya, bislee → bisleeya.

nodes.name: Past Tense Verb Endings
nodes.description: For the past tense there are five endings: -ay/-ey (1SG/3SG.M), -tay/-tey (2SG/3SG.F), -nay/-ney (1PL), -teen (2PL), -een (3PL/2PL variant). These are built from compounding: -t- signals 2nd person and 3rd feminine, -n signals 1st person plural, -ay/-ey signals past tense except for -een.

nodes.name: Seven Verbal Pronouns
nodes.description: There are seven verbal pronouns that fuse with classifiers: aan (I), aad (you SG), uu (he), ay (she/they), aannu (we excl), aynu (we incl), aydin (you PL). When added to waa, only w- is left.

nodes.name: Pronoun Fusion with waa
nodes.description: When verbal pronouns are added to the declarative classifier waa, only w- remains: waan (waa+aan), waad (waa+aad), wuu (waa+uu), wey (waa+ay), waannu (waa+aannu), weynu (waa+aynu), weydin (waa+aydin).

nodes.name: Pronoun Fusion with baa
nodes.description: When verbal pronouns are added to the focus classifier baa, only b- remains: baan (baa+aan), baad (baa+aad), buu (baa+uu), bey (baa+ay), baannu (baa+aannu), beynu (baa+aynu), beydin (baa+aydin).

nodes.name: Pronoun Fusion with ma
nodes.description: When verbal pronouns are added to the interrogative ma, only m- remains: maan (ma+aan), maad (ma+aad), muu (ma+uu), mey (ma+ay), maannu (ma+aannu), meynu (ma+aynu), meydin (ma+aydin).

nodes.name: Subject Marker -u
nodes.description: The suffix -u marks the SUBJECT case on nouns and pronouns: magacaygu (my name), adigu (you-SUBJ).

nodes.name: Definite: New vs Given Information
nodes.description: Somali distinguishes two kinds of definite information: new (just being introduced, marked by -a/-ka/-ta) and given (known or already discussed, marked by -ii/-kii/-tii).

nodes.name: Natural vs Grammatical Gender
nodes.description: Names follow natural gender (man's name = masculine, woman's name = feminine). Many nouns follow meaningful patterns. However, Somali is based on grammatical gender where assignment is arbitrary: e.g., beri (day) is masculine, maalin (day) is feminine.

nodes.name: Verb Categories
nodes.description: Each Somali verb has the following characteristics: Person (1st, 2nd, 3rd), Gender (masculine vs feminine, only on 3rd singular), Number (singular vs plural), Tense (past, present, habitual), and Conjugation (based on imperative singular ending: consonant-final = Conj 1, vowel-final = Conj 2-3, irregular = Conj 4-5).

nodes.name: baan is baa + aan
nodes.description: baan is the result of FUSION of baa (the Focus marker) and the PRONOUN aan (I).

nodes.name: Homonyms Distinguished by Gender
nodes.description: Sometimes gender is used to keep words that would otherwise be identical distinct: hal (/sha) = female camel vs hal (ka) = one; waa = declarative marker vs waa (ga) = time, era.

nodes.name: Feminine Occupation Suffix -ad
nodes.description: Feminine occupation forms have the suffix -ad: askariyad (female soldier), dhabbaakhad (female cook), dhakhtarad (female doctor), karraaniyad (female clerk), macallimad (female teacher).

nodes.statement: Factitive suffix -ee transforms nouns or adjectives into verbs with general sense of to make become X. There is no consistent change in meaning, although there is a general sense of to be X, to become X, or to make something become X.
Autobenefactive suffix -so generally denotes to do X to or for oneself. In some cases the English translation does not always contain for oneself.
Adjectival (passive) verbs follow the pattern: TRANSITIVE VERB > DERIVED ADJECTIVE + -an > ADJECTIVAL VERB with -may suffix, meaning get Xed or become X.
The conjunction oo is used to link equal sentence parts, appositive constructions, and indefinite restrictive constructions.
In several dialects ee can be substituted for oo with no difference in meaning or function.
Relative clauses take the reduced verb endings associated with SUBJECT/FOCUS verbs.
Prepositions fuse with pronouns and with each other to form combined portmanteau forms. Two-place and three-place combinations exist.

The negative conditional would not have uses prefix ma-/me- with person-specific endings: maanan (1sg), maadan (2sg), muusan (3sg.m), meeyan (3sg.f), maannan (1pl.excl), meynan (1pl.incl), meydnan (2pl), meeyan (3pl), followed by the verb root with -een suffix.

The -na suffix with negative meaning all by itself. If a verb is added, another negative marker will also be used. It attaches to nouns to create universal negative meaning: ninna (no one), meelna (nowhere), marna (never), waxna (nothing).
Oon is the fusion of oo and aan, used to mean without or although not. It creates subordinate clauses of concession or condition.
The negative imperative uses the prefix ha- before the verb stem with -in suffix for singular and -ina for plural.
The negative ma with the verb to be (ahayn) is used for predicative negation: NP + maaha (is not).
Negative focus pronoun forms combine focus marker (baa) + negative pronoun: Cali keliya baanan arkin (only Ali I did not see).
Many verb roots from Conjugation One can be used alone as masculine nouns (mostly Declension 2) with similar meaning or sense of act of Xing.
The suffix -id forms feminine nouns (Declension 1) from Conjugation One stems with the general meaning act of Xing or -ion. Sound changes affect some derivations.
The suffix -is forms feminine nouns (Declension 1) from Conjugation One stems with the meaning act of Xing, as an alternate to -id.
The suffix -in forms feminine nouns from Conjugation Two-A stems with the meaning act of Xing.
The suffix -asho forms generic feminine nouns from verb stems (especially Conjugation 3) with the meaning VERB-ing.
The suffix -nimo added to noun stems denotes a quality or state equivalent to English -ity, -ness, -hood or -ship. It creates feminine nouns of Declension 6.
The suffix -e added to verb roots forms masculine nouns of Declension 7 with the meaning doer of X, similar to English -er or -or.
The suffix -tan generally denotes reciprocal or mutual activity. It is very limited in use.
The suffix -tooyo is found on a limited number of nouns showing a state of being X, akin to -hood or -ship.
Noun plus verb compounds yield nouns indicating professions or habitual activities: af+yaqaan = linguist.
Noun plus adjective compounds yield nouns: bad+weyn = ocean, bad+yar = lake.
Noun + adjective compounds yield adjectives: fool+xun = ugly, hadal+badan = talkative.
Nouns of Declension 3 and verbs of Conjugation 3-B regularly lose the final vowel of the stem; this also happens in derivation of adjectives and other parts of speech.
Short vowels often change to match the vowels of a suffix or the following word.
In derivation of feminine nouns and verbs with feminine or second person endings, a stem final -l and suffix initial -t change to sh.
The addition of a suffix beginning with n to roots ending in -l results in ll and to those ending in -r results in rr.
Following consonants g, w, y and vowel i, in derivation of masculine nouns, the k changes to g.
Following all vowels (except i), in derivations of masculine nouns, the k changes to h.
The change of a to e occurs in derivation of Conjugation 2-A transitive verbs, infinitives or past negatives of Conjugation 1, and derived nouns with -is or -id.
In deriving verbs of Conjugation 2-A, the addition of -i to make a transitive or causative verb triggers a change of final -g to -j. This same process triggers a change of final -q to -j.
Two -t- sounds coming together result in consonant loss, affecting verb inflections. This mainly affects autobenefactive verb forms.
In a few derivations, after vowel loss occurs, the two middle consonants switch places.
Full pronouns have shorter versions which subtract the determiner suffix and in some cases the final vowel. These forms can only be used with conjunction suffixes like -na and -se in most dialects.
Only first and second person singular pronouns can be contracted in focus constructions: Anaa tegey = aniga + baa.
In inflection of feminine nouns and verbs of Conjugation 3 with a stem ending in -o, that vowel changes to -a- when suffixes are added.
With noun stems ending in -e, the final vowel changes to -a to match the vowel(s) in the suffix. This is a type of vowel harmony.

nodes.label: Definite article agrees with noun gender
nodes.description: Masculine nouns take -ka/-kii definite articles; feminine nouns take -ta/-tii. This is grammatical gender, not semantic.

nodes.label: Focus classifiers immediately follow the focused element
nodes.description: Focus markers (waa, baa, ayaa, waxa) immediately follow the element being focused. baa focuses on subject or non-subject; ayaa emphasizes immediately preceding word; waxa is used for cleft/focus constructions.

nodes.label: Declarative sentences use waa as focus marker
nodes.description: Simple declarative statements are marked with waa. In negative declaratives, waa is replaced by ma + aan negative forms.

nodes.label: Negation uses ma + aan + verb stem
nodes.description: Negative sentences use ma as the negative particle combined with aan forms (aan, aanan, aannu, etc.) fused with verbal pronouns.

nodes.label: Questions are formed with ma particle
nodes.description: Yes/no questions are formed with the interrogative particle ma. Content questions use interrogative words (maxay, goorma, xaggee, immisa, yaa, sidee, kee).

nodes.label: Verbs agree with subject in person, number, and gender
nodes.description: Verbs in Somali agree with their subjects in person (1st, 2nd, 3rd), number (singular, plural), and gender (masculine, feminine for 3rd singular).

nodes.label: Possessive pronouns are suffixed to the noun
nodes.description: Possessive pronouns are expressed as suffixes on the noun: -ayga/-aygu/-aygii (my M), -aad/-aada (your), -iis (his), -eed (her), -eenn (our exc), -een (our inc), -ood (their/your pl).

nodes.label: Genitive constructions place the possessor after the possessed noun
nodes.description: In genitive constructions, the possessed noun precedes the possessor. The definite article on the first noun carries genitive marking (-a instead of -u/-i for subject marking).

nodes.label: Habitual present expresses repeated or general action
nodes.description: The habitual present is used for repeated actions, general truths, and habitual behavior. It is not explicitly marked for tense but uses the basic verb stem with subject clitics.

nodes.label: Future tense is marked with doon
nodes.description: The future tense uses doon as an auxiliary following the verb stem. Negative future uses doon + ma + aan negative forms.

nodes.label: Imperative uses bare verb stem without subject marking
nodes.description: The imperative mood uses the bare verb stem without subject clitics. Negative imperative uses haa- + -n + verb stem. Directional particles soo and sii often accompany imperatives.

nodes.label: Optative is formed with haa- prefix
nodes.description: The optative mood expressing wishes or exhortations uses the prefix haa- with the verb stem. Forms include: ha (you sg), ha...een (you pl), ha...o (he/she), ha...nno (we), ha...na (they).

nodes.label: Relative clauses use verbal pronoun suffixes
nodes.description: Relative clauses in Somali are marked by special reduced verbal pronoun forms suffixed to the verb, rather than by relative pronouns.

nodes.label: Passive equivalent uses la impersonal subject
nodes.description: Somali does not have a true passive voice. Instead, it uses la 'someone, people' as an impersonal subject with active verb morphology.

nodes.label: D/T sound changes occur in conjugation
nodes.description: Sound changes involving d and t occur in verb conjugation, especially in conjugation 3 verbs with T+ change and loss of d next to t.

nodes.label: Numbers agree with noun gender
nodes.description: Numbers from 1-9 agree in gender with the noun they modify. The feminine form of 'one' is used with masculine nouns and vice versa.

nodes.label: Noun plurals follow eight declension patterns
nodes.description: Somali noun plurals follow eight declension patterns: 1 (-o), 2 (-ayaal/-ooyin), 3 (-ayaal), 4 (-aC#), 5 (-oyin), 6 (-o), 7 (-yaal), 8 (irregular). Each noun belongs to a specific declension class.

nodes.label: Verbal nouns are formed with suffixes from verb stems
nodes.description: Verbal nouns are formed with suffixes -id, -is (conj 1), -ad, -asho (conj 3), -aal, -itaan from verb stems. Agentive nouns use -e, privative nouns use -darro.

nodes.label: Final consonant may reduplicate before certain suffixes
nodes.description: Final consonants of verb stems may reduplicate (double) before certain suffixes and in certain morphological contexts.

nodes.label: Ownership is expressed with leh/lahow
nodes.description: Ownership or possession is expressed with the adjective leh 'having'. Negative is ma leh or lahow in conditional contexts.

nodes.label: Temporal clauses use marka 'when'
nodes.description: Temporal clauses expressing 'when' are introduced by marka. The verb in the temporal clause uses reduced (relative) pronoun forms.

nodes.label: Tag questions use sow ma aha
nodes.description: Tag questions seeking confirmation are formed with sow ma aha 'isn't it?'. The particle sow introduces a suppositive/rhetorical question.

nodes.label: Superlative uses u 'for'
nodes.description: The superlative degree is formed with u 'for' before the adjective, giving the sense of 'most X'. ugu combines u + ka for 'the most'.

nodes.label: Aan 'not' fuses with grammatical forms
nodes.description: The negative marker aan fuses with verbal pronouns and other grammatical forms, creating contracted negative forms.

nodes.label: Some dialects merge h and dh sounds
nodes.description: Certain Somali dialects merge or interchange the h and dh sounds, leading to variation in pronunciation.

nodes.label: Existential statements use wax 'thing'
nodes.description: Existential statements ('there is/are') use wax as a dummy subject with jir 'to exist' or a similar predicate.

nodes.label: Predicate tends to be sentence-final
nodes.description: Somali is generally predicate-final, with the main verb or predicate coming at the end of the clause or sentence.

nodes.label: Focus and non-focus forms may coexist in discourse
nodes.description: Both focus constructions (with baa/ayaa/waxa) and non-focus declaratives (with waa) may appear in the same discourse, with focus used for emphasis or new information.

nodes.label: Rhetorical questions use show particle
nodes.description: Rhetorical questions are marked by the particle show (variant of sow) combined with the -ee suffix on the verb.

nodes.label: Conditional clauses use haddii 'if'
nodes.description: Conditional clauses expressing 'if' are introduced by haddii, which fuses with verbal pronouns. The verb uses reduced forms.

nodes.label: Head nouns precede modifiers in noun phrases
nodes.description: In Somali noun phrases, the head noun precedes its modifiers (adjectives, relative clauses, possessives).

nodes.label: Short forms of 'to be' are used as suffixes
nodes.description: The verb 'to be' has short suffixal forms (-ahay, -aad, -ahay, etc.) that attach to nouns and adjectives to form predicates.

nodes.label: Verbs belong to conjugation classes 1, 2a, 2b, 3a, 3b
nodes.description: Somali verbs are classified into conjugation classes based on stem morphology. Conjugation 1: regular stems. 2a: C+y stems. 2b: C+e stems. 3a/3b: various irregular patterns with T+ changes.

nodes.label: Restrictive constructions use oo
nodes.description: Restrictive relative-like constructions are linked by oo 'while, and' rather than full relative clause morphology.

nodes.label: Privative nouns are formed with -darro suffix
nodes.description: Privative nouns expressing lack or absence are formed with the suffix -darro (declension 6), e.g., af-darro 'lack of speech'.

nodes.label: Factitive verbs are formed with -ee suffix
nodes.description: Factitive verbs meaning 'cause to be X' or 'become X' are formed with the suffix -ee added to adjective or noun stems.

nodes.label: Autobenefactive verbs use -at suffix
nodes.description: Autobenefactive verbs expressing action done for oneself use the suffix -at (becomes -o in some contexts).

nodes.label: Softened indirect commands use optative
nodes.description: Indirect or softened commands are expressed using optative mood forms rather than direct imperatives.

nodes.label: Appositives follow the noun they modify
nodes.description: Appositive noun phrases providing additional information follow the noun they modify, without special marking.

nodes.label: Emphatic pronouns use -na suffix
nodes.description: Emphatic forms of independent pronouns are created by adding -na 'and, also': aniga+na=anigana 'and me', iyada+na=iyadana 'and her'.

nodes.label: First person plural distinguishes inclusive and exclusive
nodes.description: First person plural pronouns distinguish inclusive (including addressee: annagu 'we all') and exclusive (excluding addressee: ayaannu 'we but not you').

nodes.label: Articles, demonstratives, and verbs agree with noun gender
nodes.description: Grammatical agreement operates between nouns and their articles (-ka/-ta), demonstratives (kani/tani), and verbal pronouns (uu/ay).

nodes.label: Different words are used for 'one' with masculine vs feminine nouns
nodes.description: The numeral 'one' has different forms depending on the gender of the noun it modifies: mid/kow/t.

nodes.label: Numbers can be joined to nouns with oo
nodes.description: Numbers above 9 can be joined to nouns with the conjunction oo 'and', forming a compound-like construction.

nodes.label: Verbal nouns from conjugation 1 use -id/-is
nodes.description: Verbal nouns derived from conjugation 1 verbs use the suffixes -id and -is (both masculine gender). Conjugation 3 verbal nouns use -ad/-asho (feminine).

nodes.label: Vocative forms use -ow/-eeyo suffix
nodes.description: Vocative forms of nouns use the suffix -ow (masculine) or -eeyo (feminine) to address someone directly.

constructions.name: Focus with baa/ayaa
constructions.example: Gabadhu bariis baa bay cuntay. (The girl ate THE RICE.)

constructions.name: Subject Focus Construction
constructions.example: Gabadhaa bariis cuntay. (THE GIRL ate the rice.)

constructions.name: Verb Focus Construction
constructions.example: Gabadhu bariis bay cuntay. (The girl ATE the rice.)

constructions.name: waxaa Focus Construction
constructions.example: Bill wuxuu yimi Djibouti. (As for Bill, he came to Djibouti.)

constructions.name: Future Tense Construction
constructions.example: Waan heli doonaa. (I will find it.)

constructions.name: Habitual Past Construction
constructions.example: Waan baran jiray. (I used to learn it.)

constructions.name: Negative Imperative Construction
constructions.example: Ha karin! (Do not cook!)

constructions.name: Negative General Past Construction
constructions.example: Maan cunin. (I did not eat it.)

constructions.name: Negative General Present Construction
constructions.example: Ma cuno. (He does not eat it.)

constructions.name: Passive Construction with la
constructions.example: Buugii cusub baa la i tusay. (I was shown the new book.)

constructions.name: Present Progressive Construction
constructions.example: joogsanayaa (I am stopping)

constructions.name: Past Progressive Construction
constructions.example: Waan cunayay. (I was eating it.)

constructions.name: Genitive Construction
constructions.example: biuggii Maxamed (Maxamed's book)

constructions.name: Adjective with Possessed Noun Construction
constructions.example: qalinka cusub ee macallinka (the new pen of the teacher)

constructions.name: Number with Noun Construction
constructions.example: saddex buug (three books)

constructions.name: What-Question Construction
constructions.example: Maxaad sameysay? (What did you do?)

constructions.name: Want-to Construction with rab
constructions.example: Bariis baan cuni rabaa. (I want to eat rice.)

constructions.name: Able-to Construction with kar
constructions.example: Af Soomaaliga baan ka hadli karaa. (I can speak Somali.)

constructions.name: Fail-to Construction with waa
constructions.example: Waan cuni waayay. (I failed to eat it / I did not eat it.)

constructions.name: Demonstrative Suffix Construction
constructions.example: gabadhan (this girl)

constructions.name: Full Possessive Suffix
constructions.description: Noun + possessive marker + definite article suffix showing case
constructions.example: magac-ayg-u (my name-SUBJ)

constructions.name: Short Possessive Suffix
constructions.description: Noun + possessive marker without definite article, used with body parts and relatives
constructions.example: hooyad-ay (my mother)

constructions.name: Prepositional Phrase with Possessive
constructions.description: Noun + position noun + possessive suffix to form prepositional meaning
constructions.example: daarta gudah-ayda (inside the house)

constructions.name: Genitive with Possessive Suffix
constructions.description: Alternative genitive: possessed noun + possessor's possessive suffix
constructions.example: macallinka buugg-iisa (the teacher his-book)

constructions.name: Negative Present Progressive
constructions.description: ma + verb stem + ay + negative present endings (o/to/no/daan)
constructions.example: Ma keen-ay-sid (You are not bringing)

constructions.name: Negative Present Progressive (Auxiliary)
constructions.description: Infinitive + maayo/maysid/mayso/etc. auxiliary
constructions.example: Waqad qorin maayay (I am not writing a letter)

constructions.name: Negative Past Progressive
constructions.description: ma + verb stem/infinitive + ayn or aynin
constructions.example: Maydin cunayn (You pl. were not eating)

constructions.name: waxa Focus Construction
constructions.description: waxa + verbal pronoun + verb + focused noun phrase
constructions.example: Waxaan cunay bariis (I am eating RICE)

constructions.name: waxa Focus Construction (Subject Focused)
constructions.description: Focused subject (absolutive) + waxa (no subject pronoun) + reduced paradigm verb
constructions.example: Kibista waxa cuna shimbiraha (The BIRDS eat the bread)

constructions.name: in-clause (Complement Clause)
constructions.description: in + subject verbal pronoun + (object) + subordinate verb form
constructions.example: in-ay iman doonaan (that they will come)

constructions.name: In Order To Construction
constructions.description: in-clause with preverbal preposition u to express purpose
constructions.example: inaan af Soomaaliga bartay (in order to learn Somali)

constructions.name: Have To / Must Construction
constructions.description: waa in + subordinate clause to express obligation
constructions.example: Waa in la cunaa (One must eat)

constructions.name: Pronoun-Preposition Cluster
constructions.description: Fixed-order cluster: PRONOUN + PREPOSITION(S) written as one word
constructions.example: kaaga (ka + a + ga = from + for + you)

constructions.name: Restrictive Relative Clause
constructions.description: Head noun + oo + clause with subordinate verb form
constructions.example: naagtan oo buugga iibsatay (the woman who bought the stamps)

constructions.name: Appositive Relative Clause
constructions.description: Head noun + ee + clause; adds supplementary info; cannot use undefined head nouns
constructions.example: ninkaan, ee Maxamed la yidhaahdo (this man, who is called Maxamed)

constructions.name: Relative Clause (Head Noun Not Subject)
constructions.description: When head noun is not subject of RC: subordinate verb forms used
constructions.example: buugga ay qortay (the book which she wrote)

constructions.name: Relative Clause (Head Noun Subject)
constructions.description: When head noun is subject of RC: reduced paradigm used
constructions.example: nimanka keenaya (the men who are bringing it)

constructions.name: Independent Pronoun
constructions.description: Pronoun base + definite article suffix (absolutive); subject form changes article ending
constructions.example: aniga (I), adiga (you), isaga (he)

constructions.name: While Construction
constructions.description: Independent pronoun + oo + appositive relative clause verb
constructions.example: Anigoo jidka soo marayay (While I was walking along the street)

constructions.name: Predicative Adjective with yahay
constructions.description: Subject + adjective + full or shortened form of yahay
constructions.example: Ninku waa dheer yahay / Ninku waa dheeryay (The man is tall)

constructions.name: Attributive Adjective in Relative Clause
constructions.description: Adjective directly modifies noun; zero/nothing absolutive, -i subject form of yahay
constructions.example: naagta dheeri (the tall woman), ninka macallinka ah (the man who is a teacher)

constructions.name: Comparative Construction
constructions.description: Subject + ka + adjective + yahay to compare two items
constructions.example: Shandaddani way ka culus tahay (This suitcase is heavier)

constructions.name: Superlative Construction
constructions.description: Subject + ugu + adjective + yahay for superlative
constructions.example: Hudheelkanu waa ugu weynyahay (This hotel is the largest)

constructions.name: Very + Adjective Construction
constructions.description: aad (focused with baa/ayaa) + ii + adjective for 'very'
constructions.example: Aad baan u fiicanahay (I am very well)

constructions.name: Which Question
constructions.description: Noun + -kee (m.) / -tee (f.) suffix, usually focused
constructions.example: Buuggee baad heshay? (Which book did you find?)

constructions.name: Where Question
constructions.description: xaggee or halkee with -kee suffix, or mee on its own
constructions.example: Xagge baydin tegi doontaan? (Where will you go?)

constructions.name: Prefixing Verb General Past
constructions.description: Person marker prefix + stem + number ending (y/t/n + imi + optional ending)
constructions.example: y-imi (he came), t-imi (you sg. came), n-imi (we came)

constructions.name: Prefixing Verb General Present
constructions.description: Person marker prefix + stem + present ending (-daa, -daan, etc.)
constructions.example: y-imaad-daa (he comes), n-imaad-naa (we come)

constructions.name: yahay General Past
constructions.description: No person prefix; person marker appears as suffix: ah + person + ending
constructions.example: ah-aa (I/he was), ah-ayd (you/she was)

constructions.name: yahay General Present
constructions.description: Person prefix + ah + ay ending; stem changes to i in 2nd/3rd plural
constructions.example: -ah-ay (I am), y-ah-ay (he is), t-ah-iin (you pl. are)

constructions.name: Comparative Adjective Construction
constructions.description: Comparative construction using preverbal preposition ka with adjective

constructions.name: Superlative Adjective Construction
constructions.description: Superlative construction using preverbal preposition cluster ugu with adjective

constructions.name: Very Intensifier Construction
constructions.description: Very intensifier with aad focused using baa/ayaa + preverbal preposition i

constructions.name: Mass Noun with Measure
constructions.structure: NOUN-UNIT ah (or: NUMBER NOUN-UNIT oo NOUN ah)
constructions.description: Mass nouns used with measure units in relative clause with ah

constructions.name: Which Question Construction
constructions.description: Which questions formed with -kee/-tee suffix, usually focused

constructions.name: Where Question Construction
constructions.description: Where questions using xaggee or halkee; answer must focus the location

constructions.name: When Adverbial Relative Clause
constructions.description: When expressed by marka with relative clause and subject verbal pronoun attached

constructions.name: After Clause Construction
constructions.description: After expressed by kaddib markuu with relative clause

constructions.name: As Soon As Clause Construction
constructions.description: As soon as expressed by isla marka with relative clause

constructions.name: Since Clause Construction
constructions.description: Since expressed by tan iyo goortii along with a relative clause

constructions.name: Although Clause Construction
constructions.description: Although expressed by in kasta plus appositive relative clause; may contract to in kasto

constructions.name: While Clause Construction
constructions.description: While expressed by intii with relative clause; head noun may merge with pronoun

constructions.name: Conditional with Haddii
constructions.description: If conditional using haddii (lit. 'the time') with relative clause; may be contracted

constructions.name: Negative Subordinate Clause
constructions.description: Negative in subordinate clauses uses aan with shortened subject pronouns attached

constructions.name: Focused Yes-No Question
constructions.structure: Ma NP baa ...? OR NP miyaa + PRON ...?
constructions.description: Two ways to focus NP in yes-no questions: baa or miyaa form

constructions.name: Negative Question with Sew
constructions.description: Negative questions without focus use sew...ma

constructions.name: Focused Negative Question
constructions.description: Focused negative question uses aan added to focus marker with shortened pronouns

constructions.name: Optative Mood (Positive)
constructions.structure: PRON VERB-ENDING (or: ha VERB-ENDING for 3rd person)
constructions.description: Optative mood for 1st/3rd person commands or wishes; ha for 3rd person

constructions.name: Optative Mood (Negative)
constructions.description: Negative optative uses invariable verb form with negative words incorporating subject pronouns

constructions.name: Potential Mood Construction
constructions.description: Potential mood expressing possibility; classifier shuw always present

constructions.name: Maybe/Perhaps Construction
constructions.description: Alternative way to express maybe/perhaps with in-clauses

constructions.name: Conditional 'Would Have'
constructions.description: Conditional 'would have' using infinitive + leh with contracted yahay forms; no tense distinction

constructions.name: Negative Conditional 'Would Have'
constructions.description: Negative conditional uses ma + infinitive + negative endings

constructions.name: Yahay Shortened Main Clause
constructions.structure: SUBJ waa ADJ-yahay (full) OR SUBJ waa ADJ-ay (shortened)
constructions.description: Shortened forms of yahay optional in main clauses, obligatory in subordinate clauses with adjectives

constructions.name: Impersonal/Pasive Construction with la
constructions.structure: ... baa la VERB ... (passive with impersonal la)
constructions.description: Impersonal pronoun la used for passive-like constructions; clusters behave like na

constructions.name: In Order To Construction
constructions.description: Purpose clause with in + subjunctive verb form

constructions.name: Focus Construction with baa
constructions.description: Noun + baa/buu/bey/etc + Verb/Adjective. The focus marker follows the focused constituent.
constructions.example: Hilib (kii) baan arkay. 'I saw some/(the) meat.'

constructions.name: Declarative Construction with waa
constructions.description: waa + Predicate. The declarative marker precedes the predicate.
constructions.example: Waa buug. 'It is a book.'

constructions.name: Yes/No Question Construction with ma
constructions.description: ma + Noun + baa. The question marker precedes the rest of the question.
constructions.example: Ma buug baa? 'Is it a book?'

constructions.name: Definite Masculine Noun (New Information)
constructions.description: Masculine noun + -ka suffix for newly introduced information.
constructions.example: dhakhtarka 'the doctor (new info)'

constructions.name: Definite Masculine Noun (Known Information)
constructions.description: Masculine noun + -kii suffix for previously known information.
constructions.example: dhakhtarkii 'the doctor (known info)'

constructions.name: Definite Feminine Noun (New Information)
constructions.description: Feminine noun + -ta suffix for newly introduced information.
constructions.example: naagta 'the woman (new info)'

constructions.name: Definite Feminine Noun (Known Information)
constructions.description: Feminine noun + -tii suffix for previously known information.
constructions.example: naagtii 'the woman (known info)'

constructions.name: Masculine Demonstrative Proximal
constructions.description: Demonstrative suffix -kan on masculine noun indicating 'this'.
constructions.example: Dhakhtarkii waa kan. 'The doctor is here.'

constructions.name: Feminine Demonstrative Proximal
constructions.description: Demonstrative suffix -tan on feminine noun indicating 'this'.
constructions.example: Naagtii waa tan. 'The woman is here.'

constructions.name: Singular Imperative
constructions.description: Bare verb stem used as command to singular addressee.
constructions.example: Cuntada keen. 'Bring the food.'

constructions.name: Plural Imperative
constructions.description: Verb stem + -a (or -ya for vowel-final verbs) used as command to plural addressees.
constructions.example: Cuntada keena. 'Bring the food. [to group]'

constructions.name: Past Tense 1st Person Singular
constructions.description: Subject + waan/baan/maan + Verb-ay/-ey.
constructions.example: Buugga waan qorey. 'I wrote the book.'

constructions.name: Past Tense 2nd Person Singular
constructions.description: Subject + waad/baad/maad + Verb-tay/-tey.
constructions.example: Buugga maad qortey? 'Did you write the book?'

constructions.name: Past Tense 3rd Person Masculine Singular
constructions.description: Subject + wuu/buu/muu + Verb-ay/-ey.
constructions.example: Buugga buu qorey. 'He wrote the book.'

constructions.name: Past Tense 3rd Person Feminine Singular
constructions.description: Subject + wey/bey/mey + Verb-tay/-tey.
constructions.example: Buugga mey qortey? 'Did she write the book?'

constructions.name: Past Tense 1st Person Plural Exclusive
constructions.description: Subject + waannu/baannu/maannu + Verb-nay/-ney.
constructions.example: Buugga waannu qorney. 'We [excl] wrote the book.'

constructions.name: Past Tense 1st Person Plural Inclusive
constructions.description: Subject + weynu/beynu/meynu + Verb-nay/-ney.
constructions.example: Buugga weynu qorney. 'We [incl] wrote the book.'

constructions.name: Past Tense 2nd Person Plural
constructions.description: Subject + weydin/beydin/meydin + Verb-teen.
constructions.example: Buugga meydin qorteen? 'Did you [pl] write the book?'

constructions.name: Past Tense 3rd Person Plural
constructions.description: Subject + wey/bey/mey + Verb-een.
constructions.example: Haa, wey qoreen. 'Yes, they wrote.'

constructions.name: Basic Greeting Exchange
constructions.description: Ma nabad baa? / Waa nabad. or Maxaad sheegtey? / Waa nabad.
constructions.example: Ma nabad baa? Waa nabad. 'How are you? Fine.'

constructions.name: Name Inquiry Construction
constructions.description: Magac-ayga/-aaga/-iisa/-eeda with waa response.
constructions.example: Magacaygu waa Yuusuf. 'My name is Joseph.'

constructions.name: Masculine Noun Vowel Harmony (-e stems)
constructions.description: Nouns ending in -e change the vowel to match the article suffix: -a with -ha (new), -i with -hii (known).
constructions.example: fure → furaha / furihii

constructions.name: Masculine Noun Vowel Harmony (-o stems)
constructions.description: Nouns ending in -o change the vowel to match the article suffix: -a with -ha (new), -i with -hii (known).
constructions.example: biyo → biyaha / biyihii

constructions.name: Feminine Noun Vowel Harmony (-o stems)
constructions.description: Feminine nouns ending in -o change the vowel to -a: -a with -da (new), -a with -dii (known).
constructions.example: cunto → cuntada / cuntadii

constructions.name: l + t → sh Assimilation
constructions.description: When a feminine noun ends in -l, the l and t of the suffix merge to -sh-.
constructions.example: basal + ta → basasha

constructions.name: k → g Assimilation
constructions.description: After nouns ending in -g, -w, -y, -i, the masculine article -ka becomes -ga.
constructions.example: buug + ka → buugga

constructions.name: k Drops After Certain Consonants
constructions.description: After nouns ending in -c, -h, -q, -kh, -x, the k of the article drops.
constructions.example: madax + ka → madaxa

constructions.name: Pronoun Fusion with waa
constructions.description: waa + pronoun → fused declarative form (only w- remains).
constructions.example: waa + aan → waan 'I [declarative]'

constructions.name: Pronoun Fusion with baa
constructions.description: baa + pronoun → fused focus form (only b- remains).
constructions.example: baa + aan → baan 'I [focus]'

constructions.name: Pronoun Fusion with ma
constructions.description: ma + pronoun → fused question form (only m- remains).
constructions.example: ma + aan → maan 'I [question]'

constructions.name: Feminine Occupation Formation
constructions.description: Masculine occupation noun + -ad → feminine counterpart.
constructions.example: macallin + ad → macallimad 'female teacher'

constructions.name: Past Tense Declarative
constructions.description: Declarative past tense with waa + verbal pronoun + past verb

constructions.name: Past Tense Focus
constructions.description: Focus past tense with baa + verbal pronoun + past verb

constructions.name: Past Tense Question
constructions.description: Past tense question with ma + verbal pronoun + past verb

constructions.name: Object Pronoun Construction

chunks.text: Pages 36-70 of Colloquial Somali cover: plural adjective formation (reduplication), genitive case constructions with suffixes -eéd/-od/-aad, numbers with nouns and their genitive rules, variants of 'one' (kow/hal/mid), verbs that lose vowels before vowel endings (maqal/maql-), irregular plurals from Arabic, general present tense paradigms for conjugations 1/2A/2B, preverbal prepositions (u/ku/ka/la), verbal object pronouns, present progressive tense formation, ordinal numbers with -aad, question word max- with subject pronouns, focus markers baa/ayaa (interchangeable), subject focus with reduced verb paradigm and absolutive case, contractions of baa (ninkaa), conjugation 3B verb formation, numbers above 10 and time expressions, infinitive formation with sound changes, future tense with doon auxiliary, habitual past with jir auxiliary, negative imperative with ha, negative general past with ma, negative general present, past progressive tense, demonstrative suffixes (-kan/-kaas/-keer/-koo), auxiliary verbs rab/kar/waa, impersonal pronoun la for passive constructions, and the Somali naming system.

Possessive suffixes have full forms with definite article and short forms without. Full forms: kayga/tayda (my), kaaga/taada (your), kiisa/tiisa (his), keeda/teeda (her), keenna/teenna (our incl.), kayaga/tayada (our excl.), kiinna/tiinna (your pl.), kooda/tooda (their). Short forms used with body parts and relatives: hooyaday, aabbahay, fartay.

Prepositional phrases formed with possessive suffixes: gudahayda/debeddeeda (inside/outside), agtiisa/agteeda (near), dishiisa/diisheeda (on top), hoostiisa/hoosteeda (beneath), geestiisa/geesteeda (at the side), hortiisa/horteeda (in front), dabadiisa/dabadeeda (behind), dartiisa/darteeda (because of), dhexdooda (among). Each has masc/fem form matching the associated noun.

Negative present progressive (conjugation 1): keenayda/keenaysid/keenaya/keenaysa/keenayna/keenaysaan/keenayaan. Alternative: infinitive + maayo/maysid/mayso/mayno/maysaan/maayaan. Past progressive negative: stem+ayn or stem+aynin (conj 1), infinitive+ayn/in (conj 2-3).
Five prefixing verbs: yiil (to be in a place, inanimate), yimi (to come), yidhi (to say), yiqiin (to know), yahay (to be). Person markers are prefixes: y- (he), t- (you/she), n- (we), zero (I).

waxa focus construction: waxa + verbal pronoun + verb + focused noun phrase. Same meaning as baa/ayaa focus but used when NP is long (e.g., incorporates relative clause). Word order differs: WAXA (+verbal pronoun) VERB FOCUSED NP. When subject focused: subject in absolutive, reduced paradigm verb, waxa lacks subject pronoun.

Subordinate clauses: (1) all essentially noun phrases; (2) no mood classifiers or focus markers; negative word is aan instead of ma; (3) special verb forms; (4) all subordinate clauses are essentially relative clauses. Three groups: in-clauses, relative clauses, and adverbial clauses.

in-clauses (complement clauses): in + subject verbal pronoun + object + verb. Used for English 'that' clauses, 'in order to', and 'have to/must'. Subordinate verb forms: present/present progressive same as main clause negative forms (-aa->-o, -aan->-aan). Past: same as main clause with different stress-tone.

Preposition-pronoun clusters: fixed order PRONOUN + u + ku + ka + la. Single stress-tone on final vowel. Examples: ii (me+for), igu (me+in), iga (me+from), ila (me+with), kuu (you+for), kugu (you+in), kaa (from+you), kula (you+with). Preposition-preposition clusters also exist: ug, uga, ula, kaga, kula, kala.

Restrictive relative clauses use oo; appositive (non-restrictive) use ee. oo is not a relative pronoun. Appositive RCs cannot be used with undefined head nouns. Restrictive RCs may not be used with names. oo marks the clause type only.

RC verb forms depend on two factors: (1) whether head noun is subject of RC, and (2) whether head noun+RC is subject of main sentence. Four possibilities total. When HN not subject of RC + RC not subject: present=main clause negative forms, past=stress on final vowel. When HN not subject + RC is subject: same as main clause forms. When HN is subject + RC not subject: reduced paradigm absolutive. When HN is subject + RC is subject: reduced paradigm subject.

Question words: goorma (when), sidee (how), yaa (who, subject, uses reduced paradigm), kuma/tuma (who, object), maxay (what), maxaad...u (why/for what), xaggee/halkee/mee (where), -kee/-tee (which), immisa/meeqaa/intee (how many/how much). Answers must focus the requested information.

Independent pronouns: aniga (I), adiga (you sg.), isaga (he/it m.), iyada (she/it f.), innaga (we incl.), annaga (we excl.), idinka (you pl.), iyaga (they). Can stand alone, used for emphasis and focusing. Shortened forms (an, ad, is) used when suffixes added. Used in 'while' construction: pronoun + oo + appositive RC.

yahay (to be): General past has no person prefix; markers as suffixes (aha, ahayd, ahayn, ahaydeen, ahaayeen). General present uses person prefixes; stem changes from ah to i in 2nd/3rd plural (ahay, tahay, yahay, tahay, nahay, tihiin, yihiin). Reduced paradigm present: ah (absolutive), ihi (subject). No progressive form (stative verb).

yahay in subordinate clauses: same forms as main clause except reduced paradigm past tense (subject form without stress-tone). With adjectives: always use contracted form (delete ah). Attributive adjectives in RCs: zero/nothing (absolutive), -i (subject form).

Common adjectives (opposites): weyn/yar (big/small), dheer/gaaban (long/short), kulul/qabow (hot/cold), dhow/fog (near/far), culus/fudud (heavy/light), wanaagsan/xun (good/bad), macaan/qadhaadh (sweet/bitter), buuran/dhuuban (fat/thin), quruxsan/fooxxin (beautiful/ugly), jirran/ladan (sick/healthy), toosan/qalloocan (straight/curved), jilicsan/adag (soft/hard), qoyan/engegan (wet/dry), dheregsan (full), harraadsan (thirsty), gaajaysan (hungry). Stress-tone on final vowel.

Comparative: ka + adjective + yahay (e.g., ka culus tahay 'is heavier than'). Superlative: ugu + adjective + yahay (e.g., ugu weynyahay 'is the largest'). Very: aad (focused with baa/ayaa) + ii + adjective. Extra emphasis: aad iyo aad.

Attributive position adjectives: hore (first, previous), dhexe (middle, between), dambe (next, last, behind), kale (other), kasta/walba (each, every), kore/sare (upper), hoose (lower), shishe (far), soke (near).
