Exercise 5: LONG vs SHORT CONSONANTS. abaar (draught) vs abbaar (aim at); beri (day) vs berri (tomorrow); caddow (become white) vs cadho (anger); caro (anger) vs carro (dirt); carrab (tongue) vs carro (dirt); gabal (portion) vs gabbal (daylight); hore (first) vs horree (precede); waran (spear) vs warran (inform); xabad (chest) vs xabbad (bullet).

Exercise 12: TONE PAIRS. ardey (student [n5-m-sg]) vs ardey (students [n5-f-pl]); awr (male camel [n5-m-sg]) vs awr (male camels [n5-f-pl]); dibi (ox [n5-m-sg]) vs dibi (oxen [n5-f-pl]); ey (dog [n5-m-sg]) vs ey (dogs [n5-f-pl]); gees (horn [n2-m]) vs gees (side [n0-f]); inan (boy [n2-m]) vs inan (girl [n2-f]); islaan (old man [n2-m]) vs islaan (old woman [n2-f]); Soomaali (a Somali [n5-m-sg]) vs Soomaali (Somalis [n5-f-pl]).

GRAMMATICAL NOTES. The three most important grammatical markers come up in this lesson: Ma marks POSITIVE (non-negative) QUESTIONS; Baa marks FOCUS (new or emphasized information); Waa marks positive (non-negative) DECLARATIVE STATEMENTS. Note the WORD ORDER: baa comes after the head noun, whereas waa comes before the head noun. The pronoun adigu is the SUBJECT (-u) FORM of adiga, and waan is the DECLARATIVE FORM of aniga.

PRONOUNS: SUBJECT WAA FORM. aniga → anigu → waan (I); adiga → adigu → waad (you [sg]); isaga → isagu → wuu (he); iyada → iyadu → wey (she); annaga → annagu → waannu (we [exclusive]); innaga → innagu → weynu (we [inclusive]); idinka → idinku → weydin (you [plural]); iyaga → iyagu → wey (they).

CULTURAL NOTE. Somali NAMES consist of one's own name followed by that of one's father and one's grandfather. Thus, Cabdullaahi Axmed Ciisa means Abdullahi who is the son of Ahmed and the grandson of Issa. Somalis also greet by shaking hands, but some may maintain physical contact much longer than an American would be used to.

GRAMMAR NOTE. In this chapter the masculine noun magac (name) has the POSSESSIVE PRONOUN suffixes -ay(ga) my, -aa(ga) your, -iis(a) his, and -eed(a) her attached. The suffix -u is used to mark the SUBJECT on forms like magacaygu (my name), magaciisu (his name) and magaceedu (her name).

GRAMMATICAL NOTE. Each Somali noun has the following characteristics: GENDER - MASCULINE (k-marked) or FEMININE (t-marked); NUMBER - SINGULAR or PLURAL; DECLENSION - the way a noun is changed or inflected based on what kind of PLURAL FORM it has (as well as its gender and tone in the singular); altogether there are eight noun declensions in Somali. This means that you will ultimately have to learn four forms for each noun: (1) Singular root, (2) with article, (3) Plural form, (4) with article.

Names follow NATURAL GENDER. aabbe (/ha) father [masculine], hooyo (/da) mother [feminine], nin (ka) man [masculine], wiil (ka) boy [masculine], gabadh (dha) girl [feminine]. However, Somali is a language based on GRAMMATICAL GENDER. beri (ga) day [masculine], maalin (ta) day [feminine], magaalo (/da) town [feminine], beled (ka) town [masculine], jid (ka) road [masculine], waddo (/da) road [feminine], subax (da) morning [feminine], habeen (ka) night [masculine], lacag (ta) money [feminine], shilin (ka) shilling [masculine].

Remember that there are two kinds of DEFINITE INFORMATION: new (just being introduced in a conversation) which is marked by -a; and given (known by the speakers or already discussed) which is marked by -ii. All changes described for the ARTICLES -ka and -kii in this chapter will also apply to the DEMONSTRATIVES -kan this, -kaas that, etc.

Exercise 1-2: With masculine nouns that end in a vowel, the k-ending changes to -h-, and the vowel will match that of the suffix. So, for nouns that end in -e, change the final vowel of the root to -a and change -ka to -ha: dukaanle → dukaanlaha, hilible → hiliblaha, madaxweyne → madaxweynaha, aabbe → aabbaha, bare → baraha, buste → bustaha, fure → furaha, jaalle → jaallaha. Exercise 2: Same with -kii → -hii: dukaanle → dukaanlihii, etc.

Exercise 3-4: With masculine nouns ending in -o, change the final vowel to -a and -ka to -ha: biyo → biyaha, ilmo → ilmaha, xoolo → xoolaha, fardo → fardaha, gacmo → gacmaha, hablo → hablaha. Known info: -o → -i, -ha → -hii: biyo → biyihii, ilmo → ilmihii, xoolo → xoolihii, fardo → fardihii, gacmo → gacmihii, hablo → hablihii.

Exercise 5-6: If a masculine noun ends in -g, -w, -y, or -i, the k will change to a g: buug → buugga, ilig → iligga, rag → ragga, daw → dawga, ey → eyga, oday → odayga, askari → askariga, beri → beriga, guri → guriga, karraani → karraaniga, Soomaali → Soomaaliga, taksi → taksiga.

Exercise 7-8: If a masculine noun ends in the consonant -c, -h, -q, -kh, or -x, the k is lost, leaving only the vowel -a: dhinac → dhinaca, magac → magaca, sac → saca, rah → raha, shaah → shaaha, dhabbaakh → dhabbaakha, shiikh → shiikha, daaq → daaqa, dariiq → dariiqa, suuq → suuqa, libaax → libaaxa, madax → madaxa, wax → waxa. Known: final short a may change to i: dhinac → dhinacii/dhinicii, magac → magacii/magicii, sac → sacii/sicii, madax → madaxii/madixii, wax → waxii/wixii.

Exercise 1-2: With feminine nouns ending in -o, the t-ending changes to -d, and the vowel will match: cunto → cuntada, daawo → daawada, hooyo → hooyada, magaalo → magaalada, shaqo → shaqada, sheeko → sheekada, waddo → waddada. Known info: o→a with -dii (not parallel to masculine -i): cunto → cuntadii, daawo → daawadii, hooyo → hooyadii, magaalo → magaaladii, shaqo → shaqadii, sheeko → sheekadii, waddo → waddadii.

Exercise 3: In dialects with feminine nouns ending in -dh, the -ta suffix changes to -dha. In other dialects these words end in -r. gabadh → gabadhdha (Alt: gabarta), eedh → feedhdha (Alt: feerta), aydh → laydhdha (Alt: layrta), joodh → qoodhdha (Alt: qoorta).

Exercise 4: If a feminine noun ends in a vowel (other than -o) or with -d, -h, -kh, -x, -w, -y, or glottal stop the t changes to d: Talaada → Talaadada, duni → dunida, mindi → mindida, Soomaali → Soomaalida, bad → badda, dawlad → dawladda, dayuurad → dayuuradda, nabad → nabadda, wasakh → wasakhda, dhex → dhexda, subax → subaxda, da' → da'da, lo' → lo'da. Also applies to FEMININE OCCUPATION forms with -ad: askariyad → askariyadda, dhabbaakhad → dhabbaakhadda, dhakhtarad → dhakhtaradda, karraaniyad → karraaniyadda, macallimad → macallimadda.

Exercise 5: Words ending in -l: combination of -l plus suffix -t changes both sounds to sh: basal + ta → basasha, bil + ta → bisha, dabeyl + ta → dabeysha, dul + ta → dusha, dhal + ta → dhasha, hal + ta → hasha, il + ta → isha, meel + ta → meesha, ul + ta → usha, walaal + ta → walaasha. Also Declension 7 plurals: aabbayaal → aabbayaasha, barayaal → barayaasha, furayaal → furayaasha, ilmayaal → ilmayaasha.

GRAMMATICAL NOTE. Although the imperative is not common, the singular imperative is the main citation form for each verb; you need to know it to find a verb in a Somali dictionary. It is also the form upon which most other tenses are built. Verbs represent the most complicated area of Somali grammar. The IMPERATIVE is the simplest of seven systems for each Somali verb.

PATTERN: FORMING THE PLURAL IMPERATIVE. Add -a to the singular imperative forms: gal → gala, bax → baxa, bar → bara, sheeg → sheega, fur → fura, xir → xira, keen → keena, cun → cuna, jar → jara, dir → dira, tag → taga, qor → qora, qaada → qaada, dhig → dhiga, shid → shida, hay → haya, hel → hela. If a verb ends in an -i or -e, add -ya: sii → siiya, akhri → akhriya, kari → kariya, bislee → bisleeya, safee → safeeya, samee → sameeya.

PATTERN 1: PAST TENSE VERB ENDINGS. For the PAST TENSE there are basically five endings: -ay Alt: -ey (I / he VERBED), -tay Alt: -tey (you [sg] / she VERBED), -nay Alt: -ney (we VERBED), -teen (you [pl] VERBED), -een (they VERBED). These endings are built up or compounded: -t- signals second person singular and plural you and third person feminine singular she, -n signals first person plural we, while -ay (or its alternate -ey) signals the past tense except for -een in the second and third person plural.

PATTERN 2: VERBAL PRONOUNS. These seven VERBAL PRONOUN forms must be memorized: aan (I), aad (you singular), uu (he), ay Alt: -ay (she ALSO they), aannu Alt: -aan (we exclusive), aynu Alt: -eynu (we inclusive), aydin Alt: -aad (you plural). When added to the DECLARATIVE CLASSIFIER waa, only w- is left. These also fuse with the FOCUS CLASSIFIER baa and with the INTERROGATIVE ma.

PATTERN 3: PRONOUN FUSION WITH MA INTERROGATIVE. Muqdisho maan tagey? (Did I go?), maad tagtey? (Did you?), muu tagey? (Did he?), mey tagtey? (Did she?), maannu tagney? (Did we [excl]?), meynu tagney? (Did we [incl]?), meydin tagteen? (Did you [pl]?), mey tageen? (Did they?).

PATTERN 4: FUSION WITH THE BAA FOCUS MARKER. Muqdisho baan tagey. (I went.), baad tagtey. (You went.), buu tagey. (He went.), bey tagtey. (She went.), baannu tagney. (We [excl] ...), beynu tagney. (We [incl] ...), beydin tagteen. (You [plural] ...), bey tageen. (They went.).

Each Somali VERB has the following characteristics: PERSON (First, Second, Third), GENDER (only on third person singular: Masculine vs Feminine), NUMBER (Singular vs Plural), TENSE (Past, Present, Habitual), CONJUGATION (based on Imperative Singular ending: Consonant final = Conjugation 1, Vowel final = Conjugations 2-3, Irregular = Conjugations 4-5).

chunks.label: Appendix Two: Folktale Translations
chunks.content: English translations of thirty Somali folktales covering cultural narratives, animal fables, moral tales, and traditional stories. Each tale demonstrates Somali narrative structure, including direct quotation patterns (often unmarked), use of focus markers in dialogue, and traditional opening/closing formulas.

chunks.label: Introduction to Survival Dialogs
chunks.content: Bilingual Somali-English dialogs presenting practical conversational situations. Each dialog is preceded by a list of useful vocabulary. Dialogs cover restaurant, renting, visiting, school, doctor, market, telephone, immigration, travel, party, housework, camping, cinema/sports, post office, and beach corps scenarios.

chunks.label: Restaurant Dialog
chunks.content: Complete restaurant conversation covering seating inquiry, menu discussion, ordering food and drinks, asking about local customs (tea drinking habits), discussing dessert, and paying the bill. Key constructions: focus markers (baa, ma), habitual tense (cabbaa), passive equivalent (la cabbaa), and politeness formulas (Mahadsanid).

chunks.label: Renting a House Dialog
chunks.content: Conversation about renting a house, discussing room count, furnishings, rent, utilities (electricity, water), contract signing requirements, and hiring household staff. Key constructions: obligation (waa in-), potential mood (karnaa), focus marker (kaa in idinkaa bixinaya).

chunks.label: Visiting Somali Friends Dialog
chunks.content: Conversation about visiting a Somali home, making introductions between friends and new acquaintances, discussing background (Arizona, Somalia), education, and future plans. Key constructions: introductions (An iskiin baro), topic pronouns (Anigu, Adigu), comparative (ka kulul), superlative (ugu horeysa).

chunks.label: First Day of School Dialog
chunks.content: Dialog between a new teacher and school director, and between teacher and students. Covers introductions, classroom management instructions, roll call, and language policy. Key constructions: numbers (afartan iyo sagaal), superlative (maalintii ugu horeysa), imperative (Fariiso), obligation (waa inaad).

chunks.label: At the Doctor Dialog
chunks.content: Medical consultation dialog covering symptom description, examination, diagnosis, and prescription. Key constructions: illness expressions (Calool xanuun baan qabaa), question formation (Ma hayso...?), ability (Waxaan kuu qori karaa...).

chunks.label: At the Market Dialog
chunks.content: Market bargaining dialog about buying carved wooden birds. Covers price negotiation and payment. Key constructions: numbers (saddex shilin, labaatan iyo shan), demonstrative (shimbirtan), relative clause (geedka laga qorey).

chunks.label: Phonetic Features Reference
chunks.content: Somali phonetic features documented in grammatical index: glottal stop [hamza], pharyngeal fricatives [c] voiced and [x] voiceless, post-alveolar retroflex stop [dh], voiceless uvular stop [q], voiced alveolar trill or roll [r]. Sound changes include D/T alternations, vowel harmony, epenthesis, metathesis, and consonant reduplication.

chunks.label: Suffix Derivation Patterns
chunks.content: Comprehensive patterns for word formation suffixes: Agentive nouns use -e (declension 7, pp.408-409). Privative nouns use -darro (declension 6, p.409). Factitive verbs use -ee (pp.332-333). Causative/transitive uses -i_ (pp.331-332, 338). Autobenefactive uses -at/-o (pp.333-334, 338). Adjectives formed with -an (declension 1). Verbal nouns use -id/-is (conj 1) or -ad/-asho (conj 3). Abstract nouns use -tooyo (stative). Science/field nouns use -aqoon. Result nouns use -tin.
